title: Tracing a Bad Prediction Back to Its Knobs
key_insight: Backpropagation follows a bad result backward through the steps that made it and gives every adjustable weight its share of the correction.
body:
## Follow the Fault Backward

A toy leaves a factory with a crooked wheel. Do not blame only the last worker; trace the toy backward and ask how much each station caused the final fault.

A neural network does this after a bad prediction. Backpropagation follows the calculation backward and gives every adjustable weight a number showing its share of the error.

Backpropagation finds the correction clues; an optimizer uses them to move the weights. Repeating predict, trace, and adjust is how the network learns.
common_mistakes: Saying backpropagation directly updates the weights — it computes gradients; the optimizer applies updates.
Blaming only the final layer — earlier layers also influenced the prediction and receive their own gradients.
Thinking a large gradient means a weight is bad — it means the loss is locally sensitive to that weight.
Expecting one backward pass to finish learning — training repeats forward, backward, and update steps.
mini_exercise: For prediction `input × weight`, use input `3`, weight `2`, and target `9`. Decide whether the weight should move up or down, and explain your answer before doing any formula.
real_world_usage: When PyTorch runs `loss.backward()`, it traces through recorded tensor operations and fills each trainable parameter's `.grad` field. An optimizer such as SGD or Adam then uses those values.
explain_back_prompt: Use the factory story to distinguish the forward pass, backpropagation, and the optimizer's update.
